title: Bhai Gurdas, the man
hook: the scribe who, tradition says, was once tested and forgiven by Guru Hargobind

segments.voice: Yesterday, Mata Ganga walked to Baba Buddha with bread she'd made herself; your line was simple bread, big blessing. Today, a man the path has met before, seen up close.

A letter arrives at a king's court in Banaras, far from Punjab. It's from Guru Hargobind, and it says something strange: a thief of mine is hiding in your city. Find him, tie his hands, and send him back to me. The king's men go looking. Before they find anyone, a quiet, learned man steps forward and says: that's me. I'm the one he means. The thief is the Guru's own scribe.
screen: `A LETTER TO BANARAS.` → `FIND MY THIEF AND TIE HIS HANDS.` → `THAT'S ME.`

segments.voice: Bhai Gurdas is a name this path has met as a writer. Tradition says he wrote out the Granth as Guru Arjan dictated it, and Sikhs speak of his own Vars as a key to the Guru's word. So it's a surprise that the story Sikhs tell about him as a man is a story of failure. There's more than one version. In a well-known one, Guru Hargobind sent him to Kabul with money to buy horses. He made the bargain and went into his tent to fetch the payment, and the money wasn't there. Some tellings say it had turned to stones. With the dealers waiting outside, he panicked. He was the Guru's trusted man, and he couldn't pay. So he slipped out the back of the tent and ran, all the way to Banaras, where nobody knew him. Some tellings add a reason for the test: he had come to feel sure no true Sikh could ever waver. Then came the letter about the thief. He knew at once who was meant. He gave himself up and was led back with his hands tied. Before Guru Hargobind, tradition says, he answered in verse, admitting he had failed and asking for mercy the way a child asks a parent. The Guru forgave him, and he stayed in the Guru's house until the end of his life. Sikhs didn't hide this story to protect a great name. They kept it. The man tradition credits with writing out the Granth was tested, ran, came back, and was forgiven.
screen: `THE SCRIBE AND POET.` · `SENT TO KABUL, THE MONEY GONE.` · `HE RAN TO BANARAS.` · `BROUGHT BACK, AND FORGIVEN.` · then, large: `EVEN HE WAS TESTED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who let you down in a small way recently: a late reply, a dropped promise, a moment they ran instead of facing something. Don't replay it; just see them, the way Guru Hargobind saw a frightened man with tied hands, and notice whether you've been keeping them in the thief's role. On each breath out, loosen the knot a little, and if you pray, say Waheguru with it.
Bhai Gurdas. The scribe and poet who, tradition says, failed a test, ran, came back with his hands tied, and was forgiven by Guru Hargobind.
Your line: even he was tested. Running wasn't the end of his story. Rest well.

howItsDone: Sikhs honor Bhai Gurdas as the scribe of the Granth and the author of the Vars, which are sung in gurdwaras, and they tell the story of his test and forgiveness as part of who he was.

original.note: Gurmukhi: Bhai Gurdas; Bhai, brother, is a title of respect for a learned or devoted Sikh.

chat.says: Why would Sikhs keep a story about Bhai Gurdas failing? Isn't that embarrassing?
options: They kept it: even the Guru's scribe ran, came back, and was forgiven.
It's a warning that anyone who fails once is never trusted again.
It shows he never really failed; the money turned up just in time.
chat.meaning: Sikhs didn't hide the story to protect a great name. The Guru's scribe failed, ran, gave himself up, and was forgiven.

notes: The Kabul horses, the empty money bag (or stones), the flight to Banaras, the letter to the Raja of Banaras and the return with tied hands follow the common telling; versions differ. Confirm the version.
'Some tellings add a reason for the test: that he had come to feel sure no true Sikh could ever waver' is a paraphrase of a common explanation; confirm.
Tradition links a specific Var stanza (often said to be in Var 36) to his plea for forgiveness; the script only says 'he answered in verse'. A Keeper may want to name it.
'Sikhs call them a key to the Guru's word' (Guru Arjan's description of the Vars as the key, kunji, to gurbani): confirm wording.
'Stayed in the Guru's house until the end of his life': confirm.
